claim: Neural and experiential effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) are attributable to agonism of the serotonin-2A receptor.
source: Previously, using pharmacological neuroimaging, we found that neural and experiential effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) are attributable to agonism of the serotonin-2A receptor (Preller et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Preller et al., 2018).

claim: The model captures the inter-areal topography of LSD-induced changes in cortical blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) functional connectivity.
source: Our model captures the inter-areal topography of LSD-induced changes in cortical blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) functional connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 2.

claim: Serotonin-2A-mediated modulation of pyramidal-neuronal gain is a circuit mechanism through which LSD alters cortical functional topography.
source: These findings suggest that serotonin-2A-mediated modulation of pyramidal-neuronal gain is a circuit mechanism through which LSD alters cortical functional topography.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling results showing that gain modulation biased toward excitatory populations best captures empirical data.

claim: Individual-subject model fitting captures patterns of individual neural differences in pharmacological response related to altered states of consciousness.
source: Individual-subject model fitting captures patterns of individual neural differences in pharmacological response related to altered states of consciousness.
evidence: The claim is supported by the individual-level modeling results and correlations with experiential measures shown in Figure 4.

claim: Areal differences in gene transcription, cellular architecture, and long-range connectivity patterns have been linked to areal differences in specialization of cortical function.
source: Areal differences in gene transcription, cellular architecture, and long-range connectivity patterns have been linked to areal differences in specialization of cortical function (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Hilgetag et al., 2016; Burt et al., 2018; Huntenburg et al., 2018; Demirtaş et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Serotonergic hallucinogens produce rapid and profound alterations of consciousness that are linked to widespread, stereotyped patterns of functional network disruption.
source: Serotonergic hallucinogens, in particular, produce rapid and profound alterations of consciousness that are linked to widespread, stereotyped patterns of functional network disruption (Tagliazucchi et al., 2014; Tagliazucchi et al., 2016; Lord et al., 2018; Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2013; Atasoy et al., 2017; Preller et al., 2018; Preller et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: LSD-induced disruptions of BOLD functional connectivity and concomitant changes in consciousness are extinguished by pre-treatment with ketanserin, a selective serotonin-2A receptor antagonist.
source: Recently, our group has shown that lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD)-induced disruptions of blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) functional connectivity (FC) and concomitant changes in consciousness are extinguished by pre-treatment with ketanserin, a selective serotonin-2A (5-HT2A) receptor antagonist (Preller et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior pharmacological neuroimaging work.

claim: The 5-HT2A receptor plays a critical role in LSD's mechanism of action.
source: This result suggests that the 5-HT2A receptor plays a critical role in LSD's mechanism of action (Vollenweider and Preller, 2020; Holze et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from prior experimental results and supported by citations.

claim: The regional topography of LSD-induced changes in GBC is aligned with the topography of regional expression levels of HTR2A.
source: We found that the regional topography of LSD-induced changes in GBC is aligned with the topography of regional expression levels of HTR2A, the gene which encodes the 5-HT2A receptor (Preller et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work that analyzed the correlation between GBC changes and HTR2A expression.

claim: The model comprises 180 interconnected nodes, each representing one left-hemispheric cortical parcel in the Human Connectome Project's Multi-Modal Parcellation.
source: Our model consists of 180 interconnected nodes, each of which represents one left-hemispheric cortical parcel in the Human Connectome Project's (HCP's) Multi-Modal Parcellation (MMP1.0) (Glasser et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim describes the model architecture and cites the parcellation scheme used.

claim: The model includes only one cortical hemisphere because the pharmacological fMRI data are approximately bilaterally symmetric.
source: Note that we model only one cortical hemisphere, as the pharmacological fMRI data informing the model are approximately bilaterally symmetric (Preller et al., 2018), and the gene expression data are sampled from the left hemisphere but show bilateral correspondence (Hawrylycz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is justified by citations to prior work showing bilateral symmetry in the data.

claim: Stimulation of 5-HT receptors alters the response properties and membrane excitability of mammalian cortical neurons such that neural gain is enhanced.
source: Stimulation of 5-HT receptors alters the response properties and membrane excitability of mammalian cortical neurons, such that firing rates are selectively enhanced for strongly depolarizing currents – that is, such that neural gain is enhanced (Araneda and Andrade, 1991; Andrade, 2011; Zhang and Arsenault, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: 5-HT receptor-mediated enhancement of gain is thought to be mediated specifically by the 5-HT2A receptor.
source: This 5-HT receptor-mediated enhancement or modulation of gain is thought to be mediated specifically by the 5-HT2A receptor (Zhang and Arsenault, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work and involves some speculation about mechanism.

claim: In cortex, 5-HT2A receptors are present on glutamatergic projection neurons and GABAergic interneurons.
source: In cortex, 5-HT2A receptors are present on glutamatergic projection neurons and GABAergic interneurons (Mengod et al., 2010; Burnet et al., 1995; Santana et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: GBC is pharmacologically elevated in sensory cortex, especially in visual cortex, and reduced in association cortex under LSD.
source: GBC is pharmacologically elevated in sensory cortex, especially in visual cortex, and reduced in association cortex (Preller et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior empirical findings.

claim: GBC changes correlate significantly with changes in subjects' experience of consciousness.
source: Moreover, GBC changes correlate significantly with changes in subjects' experience of consciousness, as determined by validated psychometric instruments (Studerus et al., 2010; Preller et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work that established this correlation.

claim: The model accurately captures the spatial topography of LSD-induced GBC changes.
source: We found that our model accurately captures the spatial topography of LSD-induced GBC changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling results presented in Figure 2.

claim: The distribution of 5-HT2A receptors is critical for generating the cortical topography of functional disruptions.
source: Our findings suggest that the distribution of 5-HT2A receptors is critical for generating the cortical topography of functional disruptions, and that neural gain is preferentially modulated on cortical pyramidal neurons, consistent with known neurobiology.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling results showing that HTR2A topography is necessary for model performance.

claim: Neural gain is preferentially modulated on cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Our findings suggest that the distribution of 5-HT2A receptors is critical for generating the cortical topography of functional disruptions, and that neural gain is preferentially modulated on cortical pyramidal neurons, consistent with known neurobiology.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from modeling results and is consistent with prior knowledge about receptor distribution.

claim: The model captures patterns of individual differences in drug response that predict altered states of consciousness.
source: Fitting the model at the individual-subject level, we found that the model captures patterns of individual differences in drug response that predict altered states of consciousness.
evidence: The claim is supported by the individual-level modeling and behavioral correlation results in Figure 4.

claim: The model ΔGBC map loaded most strongly onto the empirical ΔGBC map across a quasi-degenerate range of parameter values.
source: We found that the model ΔGBC map loaded most strongly onto the empirical ΔGBC map across a quasi-degenerate range of parameter values (Figure 2A, off-diagonal yellow band).
evidence: The claim is supported by the parameter sweep results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Model-empirical loadings collapse to form an approximately one-dimensional curve which peaks at positive shifts in E/I ratio.
source: We find that model-empirical loadings, when plotted as a function of fractional change in E/I ratio, collapse to form an approximately one-dimensional curve which peaks at positive shifts in E/I ratio (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gain modulation-induced changes in E/I balance are the primary mechanism through which GBC topography is altered under LSD.
source: This one-dimensional collapse suggests that gain modulation-induced changes in E/I balance are the primary mechanism through which GBC topography is altered under LSD.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling results showing the relationship between E/I ratio and model performance.

claim: LSD has a net-excitatory effect on cortical activity.
source: Moreover, the fact that the peak occurs for positive shifts in E/I balance suggests that LSD has a net-excitatory effect on cortical activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling results showing optimal fits at increased E/I ratios.

claim: Empirical network specificity of GBC changes was recapitulated in the model.
source: We found that empirical network specificity of GBC changes was recapitulated in the model (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the network-level analysis shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The statistical association between model and empirical ΔGBC was significantly stronger than the association between the HTR2A gene expression map and the empirical ΔGBC map.
source: This statistical association was significantly stronger than the association between the HTR2A gene expression map and the empirical ΔGBC map (p = 0.011; test for difference between dependent correlations) (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical comparison shown in Figure 2H.

claim: A statistically significant brain-behavior relationship between the neural and experiential effects of LSD was observed when – and only when – GSR was performed.
source: There, a statistically significant brain-behavior relationship between the neural and experiential effects of LSD was observed when – and only when – GSR was performed.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior analysis (Preller et al., 2018).

claim: When GSR was not used, the spatial correspondence of the ΔGBC map with the HTR2A expression map is dramatically attenuated.
source: Moreover, GSR was found to substantially alter the topography of the empirical ΔGBC map: when GSR was not used, the spatial correspondence of the ΔGBC map with the HTR2A expression map is dramatically attenuated (Preller et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior analysis.

claim: When GSR is not performed, maximal model-empirical loading and Spearman rank correlation between the model and empirical ΔGBC maps are both reduced significantly.
source: Here, we find that when GSR is not performed, maximal model-empirical loading and Spearman rank correlation between the model and empirical ΔGBC maps are both reduced significantly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LSD exerts predominately agonistic activity at 5-HT-2C, -1A/B, -6, and -7 receptors, as well as dopamine D1 and D2 receptors.
source: In addition to stimulating 5-HT2A receptors, LSD exerts predominately agonistic activity at (5-HT)-2C, -1A/B, -6, and -7 receptors, as well as dopamine D1 and D2 receptors (Nichols, 2004; Passie et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior pharmacological studies.

claim: Using the HTR2A map in the model yields the maximal model-empirical loading and Spearman rank correlation between empirical and simulated ΔGBC maps compared to other receptor-encoding genes.
source: Of the receptor-encoding genes that we tested, using the HTR2A map in the model yields the maximal model-empirical loading and Spearman rank correlation between empirical and simulated ΔGBC maps (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Modulating gain in proportion to HTR2A expression levels produces a statistically significant loading (p = 0.008).
source: We found that modulating gain in proportion to HTR2A expression levels produces a statistically significant loading (p = 0.008).
evidence: The claim is supported by the spatial autocorrelation-preserving surrogate map test results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: None of the alternative gene expression maps reach significance of p < 0.05 in the surrogate map test.
source: The null distribution further reveals that none of the alternative gene expression maps reach significance of p < 0.05.
evidence: The claim is supported by the surrogate map test results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Individual differences in ΔGBC are primarily driven by the strength with which subjects exhibit the group-averaged pattern.
source: This indicates that individual differences are primarily driven by the strength with which subjects exhibit the group-averaged pattern.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the strong correlation between PC1 and the group-averaged map.

claim: Variation across subjects' simulated ΔGBC maps is almost entirely captured by the two leading model PCs.
source: The model PC variance spectrum shows that variation across subjects' simulated ΔGBC maps is almost entirely captured by the two leading model PCs (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the variance spectrum analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The empirical data exhibit approximately five significant modes of variation.
source: However, the empirical PC variance spectrum reveals that the data exhibit approximately five significant modes of variation (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the permutation testing of the empirical variance spectrum shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 67% of model variance fell within the subspace defined by the data's leading five PCs.
source: A linear subspace analysis revealed that 67% of model variance fell within the subspace defined by the data's leading five PCs (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by the linear subspace analysis described in the methods.

claim: The majority of model variation lies within a low-dimensional subspace defined by the principal modes of empirical variation.
source: In other words, we found that the majority of model variation lies within a low-dimensional subspace defined by the principal modes of empirical variation.
evidence: The claim is based on the subspace analysis showing 67% overlap.

claim: Changes in conscious experience were determined psychometrically using the five-dimensional altered states of consciousness (5D-ASC) questionnaire.
source: As reported by Preller et al., 2018, changes in conscious experience were determined psychometrically using the five-dimensional altered states of consciousness (5D-ASC) questionnaire (Dittrich et al., 2010), which was administered to study participants 180 min after drug infusion.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure and is supported by citations.

claim: The 5D-ASC questionnaire quantifies changes in conscious experience along five distinct experiential dimensions: experiences of disembodiment, elemental imagery, changed meaning of percepts, blissful state, and spiritual experience.
source: The short version of the 5D-ASC questionnaire quantifies changes in conscious experience along five distinct experiential dimensions: experiences of disembodiment, elemental imagery, changed meaning of percepts, blissful state, and spiritual experience – each of which is profoundly altered under LSD (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim describes the psychometric instrument and is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There is evidence for a single dominant experiential regression map pattern.
source: How consistent are these experiential regression maps across experiential dimensions? We found evidence for a single dominant experiential regression map pattern (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by the PCA of experiential regression maps shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The model captures patterns of functional individual variation that are linked to individual differences in pharmacologically induced changes in experience.
source: This indicates that the model captures patterns of functional individual variation that are linked to individual differences in pharmacologically induced changes in experience.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the correlation between model PC1 and experiential regression patterns.

claim: The ΔGBC topography was captured in silico when LSD's effect on molecular signaling was modeled as a modulation of neuronal gain, mediated by 5-HT2A receptor agonism, with preferential impact on pyramidal neurons.
source: Here, we found that the ΔGBC topography was captured in silico when LSD's effect on molecular signaling was modeled as a modulation of neuronal gain, mediated by 5-HT2A receptor agonism, with preferential impact on pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main modeling findings.

claim: The findings were specifically attributable to the topography of the HTR2A expression map.
source: Moreover, our findings were specifically attributable to the topography of the HTR2A expression map – our transcriptomic proxy measure of the spatial distribution of 5-HT2A receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comparative analysis with other receptor maps and surrogate map testing in Figure 3.

claim: The model has enough expressivity to fit individual subjects and exhibits patterns of variation that predict drug-induced alterations of consciousness.
source: Finally, we showed that the model has enough expressivity to fit individual subjects and exhibits patterns of variation that predict drug-induced alterations of consciousness.
evidence: The claim summarizes the individual-level modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: A recent modeling study by Deco et al., 2018 showed that a gain-modulatory mechanism captures changes in global spatiotemporal properties of group-level neural dynamics under LSD but did not examine cortical topographic effects.
source: Our findings complement a recent modeling study by Deco et al., 2018, which showed that a gain-modulatory mechanism captures changes in global spatiotemporal properties of group-level neural dynamics under LSD but did not examine cortical topographic effects as studied here.
evidence: The claim describes prior work and is supported by citation.

claim: Changes in global metrics may be driven by spatially non-specific effects and by non-neuronal components or artifacts, particularly in imaging studies of serotonergic psychedelics.
source: However, changes in global metrics may be driven by spatially non-specific effects and by non-neuronal components or artifacts, particularly in imaging studies of serotonergic psychedelics (Lewis et al., 2017; Preller et al., 2018; Vollenweider and Preller, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work discussing methodological issues.

claim: Gain modulation is a molecular mechanism that explains the specific spatial topography of LSD's functionally disruptive effects.
source: Our findings here demonstrate that gain modulation is a molecular mechanism that explains the specific spatial topography of LSD's functionally disruptive effects.
evidence: The claim is based on the modeling results showing that gain modulation captures spatial topography.

claim: The best model fits are associated with elevation of E/I ratio and gain modulation that is biased toward excitatory populations.
source: Our finding that the best model fits are associated with elevation of E/I ratio and gain modulation that is biased toward excitatory populations suggests that LSD preferentially targets pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the parameter sweep results shown in Figure 2.

claim: LSD preferentially targets pyramidal neurons.
source: Our finding that the best model fits are associated with elevation of E/I ratio and gain modulation that is biased toward excitatory populations suggests that LSD preferentially targets pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling results and is consistent with prior anatomical knowledge.

claim: 5-HT2A receptors are preferentially found on apical dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons in humans, monkeys, and rats.
source: This finding converges with multiple lines of experimental evidence in humans (Pazos et al., 1987; Hall et al., 2000), monkeys (Jakab and Goldman-Rakic, 1998), and rats (Willins et al., 1997; Santana et al., 2004), which show that 5-HT2A receptors are preferentially found on apical dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies across species.

claim: 5-HT2A receptor agonists induce substantial increases in cortical pyramidal neuron firing rates.
source: Moreover, 5-HT2A receptor agonists have been shown to induce substantial increases in cortical pyramidal neuron firing rates (Martín-Ruiz et al., 2001; Puig et al., 2003; Lladó-Pelfort et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: HTR2A expression is significantly elevated in excitatory cell types, relative to inhibitory cell types, according to single-cell RNA sequencing data.
source: State-of-the-art single-cell RNA sequencing data across multiple cortical areas in humans also reveals that HTR2A expression is significantly elevated in excitatory cell types, relative to inhibitory cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Most prior models of psychedelics' pharmacological effects in humans have been fitted to group-level statistical measures.
source: Most prior models of psychedelics' pharmacological effects in humans have been fitted to group-level statistical measures (Deco et al., 2018; Preller et al., 2019; Kringelbach et al., 2020; Herzog et al., 2020; Pfeffer et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior modeling studies.

claim: By fitting to individual subjects, the model can capture experientially relevant modes of neural variation.
source: Here, we have shown that by fitting to individual subjects, the model can capture experientially relevant modes of neural variation.
evidence: The claim summarizes the individual-level modeling results.

claim: The model fits the majority of subjects well.
source: Our model fits the majority of subjects well (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the individual subject fits shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several subjects were too idiosyncratic in their neural responses for the model to accurately predict individuals' experiential responses to LSD.
source: However, the number of subjects included in the empirical data collection supporting this study was not statistically well powered for individual differences predictive analyses, and several subjects were too idiosyncratic in their neural responses for us to accurately predict individuals' experiential responses to LSD.
evidence: The claim acknowledges limitations in the individual-level modeling.

claim: LSD primarily mediates its effects on the human brain through 5-HT2A receptors.
source: LSD primarily mediates its effects on the human brain through 5-HT2A receptors (Preller et al., 2018; Holze et al., 2021), but LSD also acts as an agonist at other serotonergic and dopaminergic receptor sites (Nichols, 2004; Passie et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior pharmacological studies.

claim: LSD exhibits high affinity for 5-HT1A receptor subtypes, which function as inhibitory autoreceptors in the raphe nuclei and induce post-synaptic membrane hyperpolarization in limbic areas.
source: In particular, LSD exhibits high affinity for 5-HT1A receptor subtypes, which function as inhibitory autoreceptors in the raphe nuclei and induce post-synaptic membrane hyperpolarization in limbic areas (Filip and Bader, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior pharmacological work.

claim: 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A receptors mediate opposing influences on membrane excitability.
source: Thus, 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A receptors mediate opposing influences on membrane excitability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known functions of these receptors.

claim: Partial 5-HT1A receptor agonists have 'anti-psychedelic' properties in humans.
source: Interestingly, this bidirectionality appears consistent with the 'anti-psychedelic' properties of partial 5-HT1A receptor agonists in humans (Pokorny et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior pharmacological work.

claim: 5-HT2A receptors are found in all cortical laminae.
source: In addition, 5-HT2A receptors are found in all cortical laminae (Jakab and Goldman-Rakic, 1998; Burnet et al., 1995), often colocalized with 5-HT1A receptors on pyramidal neurons (Araneda and Andrade, 1991; Amargós-Bosch et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: 5-HT2A receptors are often colocalized with 5-HT1A receptors on pyramidal neurons.
source: In addition, 5-HT2A receptors are found in all cortical laminae (Jakab and Goldman-Rakic, 1998; Burnet et al., 1995), often colocalized with 5-HT1A receptors on pyramidal neurons (Araneda and Andrade, 1991; Amargós-Bosch et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: 5-HT2A receptors are found on GABAergic interneurons, though relatively infrequently.
source: 5-HT2A receptors are also found on GABAergic interneurons, though relatively infrequently (Willins et al., 1997; Santana et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: GS artifacts exhibit dramatic differences in clinical populations and following pharmacological manipulations.
source: In particular, GS artifacts exhibit dramatic differences in clinical populations and following pharmacological manipulations (Driesen et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2014; Power et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017; Lewis et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: Results frequently do not replicate across samples when GSR is not performed in psychedelic studies.
source: The data processing decision to include or forego GSR therefore has impact on findings in studies of psychedelics (Preller et al., 2018; Preller et al., 2020): it has been shown that results frequently do not replicate across samples when GSR is not performed (Tagliazucchi et al., 2016; Preller et al., 2018; Müller et al., 2017; Preller et al., 2020), while studies that use GSR have reported replicable findings (Preller et al., 2018; Preller et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies examining GSR effects.

claim: Studies that use GSR have reported replicable findings in psychedelic research.
source: The data processing decision to include or forego GSR therefore has impact on findings in studies of psychedelics (Preller et al., 2018; Preller et al., 2020): it has been shown that results frequently do not replicate across samples when GSR is not performed (Tagliazucchi et al., 2016; Preller et al., 2018; Müller et al., 2017; Preller et al., 2020), while studies that use GSR have reported replicable findings (Preller et al., 2018; Preller et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies examining GSR effects.

claim: Multiple measures of model-empirical similarity were significantly improved when GSR was performed.
source: Here, we found that multiple measures of model-empirical similarity were significantly improved when GSR was performed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), providing further support for its use.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spatial autocorrelation occurs ubiquitously in empirical brain maps and can dramatically inflate p-values in analyses of both cortical and subcortical brain maps.
source: Spatial autocorrelation occurs ubiquitously in empirical brain maps and can dramatically inflate p-values in analyses of both cortical and subcortical brain maps (Burt et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior methodological work.

claim: Gene expression profiles exhibit characteristic hierarchical patterns of intra-cortical variation.
source: For instance, although gene expression profiles exhibit characteristic hierarchical patterns of intra-cortical variation (Burt et al., 2018), cortico-cortical gene expression variance is small relative to cortico-subcortical variance (Hawrylycz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior transcriptomic studies.

claim: Cortico-cortical gene expression variance is small relative to cortico-subcortical variance.
source: For instance, although gene expression profiles exhibit characteristic hierarchical patterns of intra-cortical variation (Burt et al., 2018), cortico-cortical gene expression variance is small relative to cortico-subcortical variance (Hawrylycz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior transcriptomic work.

claim: Variation in gene expression levels across human brain regions generally well captured regional variation in protein expression levels.
source: Carlyle et al., 2017 found that variation in gene expression levels across human brain regions generally well captured regional variation in protein expression levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work comparing transcriptomics and proteomics.

claim: Beliveau et al., 2017 found good alignment between PET maps for serotonin receptors and gene expression levels from the AHBA.
source: Beliveau et al., 2017 directly compared PET maps for serotonin receptors and found good alignment with gene expression levels from the AHBA.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work comparing PET and transcriptomics.

claim: For many receptors of interest, PET mapping is not yet possible due to lack of developed radioligands.
source: A key limitation of using PET-derived maps for model simulations of pharmacology is that for many receptors of interest, PET mapping is not yet possible due to lack of developed radioligands (Pike, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on PET radioligand development.

claim: Transcriptomic mapping can inform large-scale models of pharmacological neuroimaging.
source: Our study demonstrates proof of concept that transcriptomic mapping can inform large-scale models of pharmacological neuroimaging.
evidence: The claim is based on the successful application of transcriptomic data in the modeling framework.

claim: The 5-HT2A receptor-rich claustrum may play a role in mediating the effects of serotonergic psychedelic drugs.
source: Moreover, while 5-HT2A receptors are predominately found in cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), future model extensions with subcortical structures can incorporate the 5-HT2A receptor-rich claustrum (Hall et al., 2000), which may play a role in mediating the effects of serotonergic psychedelic drugs (Barrett et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim involves speculation about the claustrum's role and is supported by citations.

claim: Recent years have experienced a resurgence of clinical interest in the use of psychedelics as therapeutics for the treatment of mood disorders, alcohol and substance abuse, and end-of-life distress in terminally-ill patients.
source: Recent years have experienced a resurgence of clinical interest in the use of psychedelics as therapeutics for the treatment of mood disorders, alcohol and substance abuse, and end-of-life distress in terminally-ill patients (Carhart-Harris and Goodwin, 2017; Nichols et al., 2017; Vollenweider and Preller, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior clinical research reviews.

claim: Multiple lines of evidence point to 5-HT2A receptor-mediated glutamate release as a common therapeutic mechanism of serotonergic psychedelic drugs.
source: The common therapeutic mechanism of serotonergic psychedelic drugs remains unclear, although multiple lines of evidence now point to 5-HT2A receptor-mediated glutamate release (Vollenweider and Kometer, 2010; Mason et al., 2020; Vollenweider and Preller, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior mechanistic studies.

claim: Group-averaged left-hemispheric SC matrices were constructed from diffusion MRI data using probabilistic tractography for 339 unrelated subjects from the HCP 900-subject data release.
source: Group-averaged left-hemispheric SC matrices were constructed from diffusion MRI data using probabilistic tractography for 339 unrelated subjects from the HCP 900-subject data release (Van Essen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the data source and processing method.

claim: Twenty-five healthy human participants received either placebo or LSD (100 µg po) in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject study design.
source: Briefly, fMRI data derived from a double-blind, placebo-controlled, and within-subject study design, ensuring that each subject served as their own control. Twenty-five healthy human participants received either (i) placebo or (ii) LSD (100 µg po).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and is supported by citation to the original study.

claim: Resting-state scans were collected 75 min following drug administration.
source: Resting-state scans were collected 75 min following drug administration.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental timing.

claim: One subject was excluded from analysis due to failure in registration caused by an improper head position, resulting in 24 study participants analyzed.
source: One subject was excluded from analysis due to failure in registration caused by an improper head position. Thus, 24 study participants were analyzed in this study.
evidence: The claim describes the final sample size and exclusion criterion.

claim: HTR2A is predominately expressed in cortical pyramidal neurons in the human brain.
source: In the human brain, HTR2A is predominately expressed in cortical pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HTR2A is significantly more expressed in excitatory neurons than in inhibitory neurons (W = 141,943; p < machine precision).
source: HTR2A is significantly more expressed in excitatory neurons than in inhibitory neurons (W = 141,943; p < machine precision; Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis of single-cell data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Performing GSR significantly improves the Spearman rank correlation between the HTR2A expression map and the empirical ΔGBC map (p < 10−5).
source: Performing GSR significantly improves: the Spearman rank correlation between the HTR2A expression map and the empirical ΔGBC map (left; p < 10−5; test for difference between dependent correlations); maximal model-empirical loading (center; p = 0.03; spatial autocorrelation-preserving surrogate map test); and the Spearman rank correlation between the model and empirical ΔGBC maps (right; p < 10−5; test for difference between dependent correlations).
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Performing GSR significantly improves maximal model-empirical loading (p = 0.03).
